Checking the numbers: what public salary data can and cannot tell you

Short answer: no government dataset reports pay for API 510, API 570 or API 653 inspectors as a separate job. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics puts them inside the broad "quality control inspectors" group, whose median annual wage the BLS publishes in its Occupational Outlook Handbook. Salary websites publish API-titled pages, but they mix job titles, experience levels, contract hourly rates and self-reported data. Before relying on any salary band, including the ranges above, check it against an offer and against the sources explained in this section. For a new inspector on the Gulf Coast, what sits around the API certificate (NDT qualifications, rotation and turnaround availability, and the equipment you have actually inspected) usually matters more to pay than the certificate number.

This section explains what each public source measures, why they disagree, what API ICP itself publishes, and how to answer the question new inspectors ask most often: API 510 or API 570 first, and which has steadier work along the Gulf Coast?

What the federal data says, and what it leaves out

The only federal salary source is the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Its Occupational Outlook Handbook profile for quality control inspectors reports the median annual and hourly wage for May 2025 (see the BLS profile for the current figures). The same profile counts about 602,000 jobs in 2025 and projects 3 percent employment growth from 2025 to 2035, about as fast as the average for all occupations. It also shows that pay depends on the industry: professional, scientific and technical services paid the highest median of the industries listed, and administrative and support services paid the lowest.

That figure is real, but it describes a very different group from API-certified inspectors. "Quality control inspectors" covers everyone who inspects, tests, sorts, samples or weighs. That includes final-assembly checkers in light manufacturing, food-packing samplers and incoming-goods inspectors, as well as the small group of people who sign API 510, 570 and 653 reports. Since the large manufacturing population sets the median, the BLS figure is a floor for the occupation as a whole, not an estimate of what a certified refinery inspector earns.

BLS also publishes wages by state and metro area through its Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics program, so you can compare Texas, Louisiana, Houston, Beaumont-Port Arthur, Baton Rouge or Lake Charles for the same broad category. Those comparisons help you see how wage levels differ between regions. They will not separate API inspectors from everyone else, because no standard occupational code exists for "API inspector."

Why there is no "API inspector" job code

API 510, 570 and 653 certifications are individual credentials issued by the American Petroleum Institute's Individual Certification Programs (ICP). They are not occupations. The same certificate holder might be employed as an "inspector," "mechanical integrity specialist," "QA/QC inspector," "fixed equipment inspector," "inspection coordinator" or "reliability technician," and each of those titles lands in a different place in government surveys. So for pay that applies specifically to API certificate holders, you have to rely on job postings and self-reported data, which come with their own biases.

Why salary websites disagree so much

If you search "API inspector salary," you will find pages from ZipRecruiter, Glassdoor, Indeed, Salary.com and others, often with separate pages for "API 510 inspector," "API 570 inspector" and "API 570 piping inspector." The figures differ widely between sites, and sometimes between two pages on the same site. Here is why:

  • Different inputs. Some aggregators model pay from job advertisements, which often state hourly ranges for contract work. Others rely on employees reporting their own pay. A posting-based figure follows what employers advertise. A self-reported figure follows whoever chooses to submit data, and those people are often early in their careers and looking for work.
  • Base pay versus total pay. Contract inspectors on the Gulf Coast are often paid hourly with overtime during turnarounds, and some contracts add per diem for travel. A salary site may show base pay only, total pay, or a modelled annual figure that assumes a standard 2,080-hour year. Each of these gives a different result for the same job.
  • Title mixing. An "API 570 inspector" posting may really be for a junior UT thickness technician who is expected to earn the certificate later. It may also be for a senior inspector of record at a major refinery. Both appear under the same keyword.
  • Small samples. Pages for a narrow title in one city can rest on a handful of data points. Where a site shows a sample size or a date range, check it.
  • Dates. Aggregator pages update at different times. Before you compare two figures, check the "as of" date on each page.

Treat these pages as a rough guide, not a benchmark. The questions on the employer's offer (hourly or salaried, overtime terms, per diem, rotation pattern, benefits) tell you more than any national average.

API 510 vs API 570: which pays better for a brand-new inspector on the Gulf Coast?

No public source we could verify shows that a newly certified API 510 inspector reliably earns more or less than a newly certified API 570 inspector. Pages for both titles show overlapping ranges, and employers along the Texas and Louisiana coast often ask for both certificates in the same posting. What separates two new inspectors is usually experience, NDT qualifications and availability, not which API number they hold.

The bigger question is which certification you can actually qualify for, and which one leads to work you can get. Some practical points:

  • Eligibility depends on equipment-specific experience. API's published requirements for API 510 count pressure vessel experience. API 570 counts experience with in-service metallic piping systems. API 653 counts aboveground storage tank experience. If the last few years of your work were mostly on piping circuits, API 570 may be the only one you can document today.
  • Piping is the largest population of fixed equipment. In a typical refinery or chemical plant, piping circuits and condition monitoring locations far outnumber vessels, so a lot of routine thickness and external visual work is piping work. That is a description of how plants are built, not a wage statistic, but it is why many inspection programmes need people with API 570 knowledge every day.
  • Vessel work clusters around turnarounds. Internal vessel inspections mostly happen when units are shut down, so API 510 work tends to peak during turnaround seasons. On-stream thickness and external work continues between turnarounds on both vessels and piping.
  • Neither certificate is rare. API ICP's statistics presentation for its May 2024 annual meeting charted about 20,108 API 510 and 18,491 API 570 certifications as of April 2024. With supply that similar, scarcity of one certificate is unlikely to explain much of any difference in pay. Scope, location and experience are what count.
  • Holding both is common. Many working inspectors add the second certificate once they have the experience it requires. In postings, "510/570" usually means the employer wants the combination.

So if your goal is steady work, the sensible order for most people is to earn the certification your experience already supports, then add the second when you qualify for it. For a fuller comparison of the three programmes, see API 510 vs 570 vs 653: which certification first and the side-by-side API 510 vs API 570 comparison.

What API ICP actually requires (public information)

Employers pay for a certificate only because of what it lets the holder do. Under each API code, the certified inspector is the person authorised to perform and sign the inspection functions that code defines. The requirements below are taken from API's public ICP pages for each programme. Fees, scheduling and policies change, so check the current page on api.org before you apply.

EducationAPI 510 (pressure vessels)API 570 (piping)API 653 (tanks)
BS or higher in engineering or technology1 year in supervision or performance of inspection1 year in supervision or performance of inspection1 year of inspection experience
2-year degree or certificate in engineering or technology2 years of pressure vessel experience, 1 year in inspection2 years in design, construction, repair, operation or inspection, 1 year in inspection2 years of tank experience, 1 year in inspection
High school diploma or equivalent3 years, 1 year in inspection3 years, 1 year in inspection3 years, 1 year in inspection
No formal education5 or more years, 1 year in inspection5 or more years, 1 year in inspection5 or more years, 1 year in inspection

API's pages also list military technical service as a substitute for some education levels, and they say the experience must have been gained within a recent window (the API 570 and API 653 pages state the last 10 years). The exam is the same for all three: 7.5 hours with 170 questions, of which 140 are scored, split into a 110-question closed-book section and a 60-question open-book section. It is delivered in person at Prometric test centres, and the code documents are provided as PDFs during the open-book portion. A certification lasts three years. To recertify, you must show that at least 20 percent of your working time went to inspection activities and complete 24 continuing professional development hours per cycle, plus an online quiz on code changes every six years.

Why does this matter for pay? Because the experience requirement filters out most applicants. The certificate is a signal that someone has already spent time on the right equipment, and that is what employers pay a premium for. For the eligibility detail, see API 510 certification requirements; for the three-year cycle, see API ICP recertification.

What actually moves an API inspector's pay

From public job postings and how the work is organised, these factors make the biggest difference to what an inspector is offered. None of them depends on a single published average.

1. NDT qualifications alongside the API certificate

An API certificate qualifies you to inspect and evaluate under the code. It does not qualify you to perform ultrasonic, radiographic, magnetic particle or other NDT methods. Under most employers' written practices, NDT method qualifications come from ASNT SNT-TC-1A or ANSI/ASNT CP-189 schemes. An inspector who can both evaluate to API 570 and personally perform UT thickness surveys, for example, can be used on more jobs. That is why postings often ask for "API 510/570 plus UT Level II."

2. Contract versus staff roles

Staff inspectors at an owner-operator are usually salaried with benefits and a predictable schedule. Contract inspectors placed through service companies are often hourly, work extended hours during turnarounds, and may receive travel pay. Their annual totals vary much more from year to year. When you compare offers, convert both into the same terms: hours per year, overtime rules and whether per diem is taxable.

3. Turnaround availability and travel

Turnarounds create short, intense demand for inspectors with the right certificates. People who can travel between Gulf Coast sites, or further afield, have access to more of that work. People who need to stay in one metro area depend on that area's owners and contractors.

4. Equipment and damage-mechanism experience

Experience with specific damage mechanisms counts for a lot: wet H2S service, high-temperature hydrogen attack screening, corrosion under insulation programmes, injection points and deadlegs. Familiarity with API 571 damage mechanisms and API 577 welding inspection is part of the API 510 and 570 bodies of knowledge, and real field exposure to these makes an inspector more valuable.

5. Documentation and software skills

Mechanical integrity programmes depend on records: thickness data, corrosion rates, remaining life, next inspection dates and the reasons behind each recommendation. Inspectors who produce clean, defensible reports (the kind that survive an OSHA PSM audit or a jurisdictional review) are trusted with more responsibility.

Gulf Coast context: where API inspection work comes from

The Texas and Louisiana coast has one of the densest groups of refineries, chemical plants, gas processing plants and storage terminals in North America, from Corpus Christi through the Houston Ship Channel and Beaumont-Port Arthur to Lake Charles, Baton Rouge and the Mississippi River corridor. Several regulatory drivers keep that equipment under continuous inspection:

  • OSHA Process Safety Management (29 CFR 1910.119). The mechanical integrity paragraph covers pressure vessels and storage tanks, piping systems, relief and vent systems, emergency shutdown systems, controls and pumps. It requires inspection and testing procedures that follow recognised and generally accepted good engineering practices, at a frequency consistent with manufacturers' recommendations and good engineering practice. API 510, 570 and 653 are widely treated as those practices for vessels, piping and tanks.
  • PHMSA breakout-tank rules (49 CFR 195.432). Operators of hazardous liquid pipelines must inspect atmospheric and low-pressure steel breakout tanks to API Std 653. This creates tank inspection work at pipeline terminals.
  • EPA SPCC (40 CFR 112). Facilities that store oil above the thresholds must test or inspect each aboveground container for integrity on a regular schedule and whenever material repairs are made, usually following API 653 or STI SP001.
  • State boiler and pressure vessel programmes. Texas and Louisiana each run state programmes for boilers and certain pressure vessels. Whether a given vessel falls under state inspection depends on the state's rules, so confirm with the jurisdiction.

These programmes run all year, which is why piping and tank inspection between turnarounds gives steady base demand, while turnarounds add peaks. For coast-specific NDT training context, see NDT training in Texas.

Canada note

Canadian provinces regulate pressure equipment through provincial safety authorities, such as ABSA in Alberta and TSSA in Ontario, which have their own inspector certification schemes. API certificates are recognised by many owner-users there as part of their programmes, but provincial requirements decide who may inspect equipment registered in that province. If you plan to work in Alberta's oil sands or Ontario's petrochemical clusters, check the provincial authority's inspector requirements as well as API ICP. Pay data in Canada comes from Statistics Canada and Job Bank, which use their own occupational codes and have the same "no API-specific category" problem as BLS.

More questions on API inspector pay

Between API 510 and API 570, which pays better for a brand-new inspector, and which has steadier work on the Gulf Coast?

No verified public dataset separates pay for new API 510 and API 570 inspectors, and postings often ask for both. Piping makes up most of the fixed equipment in refineries and chemical plants, so API 570 work runs all year, while API 510 internal vessel work peaks during turnarounds. Get the certificate your experience supports first.

What is a typical piping inspector salary?

"Piping inspector" covers everyone from UT thickness technicians to API 570 inspectors of record, so pay ranges are wide. Compare offers on the same basis (hourly versus salaried, overtime, per diem, benefits) and look at state and metro wage data, not national figures.

Does an API 653 certification pay more than API 510 or 570?

We found no public data showing a consistent difference. API 653 work centres on tank terminals, pipeline breakout tanks and SPCC-regulated facilities. How much tank work exists where you live matters more than the certificate number.

Do API inspectors need NDT certification too?

API certification does not qualify you to perform NDT methods. Employers usually require NDT qualifications under an SNT-TC-1A written practice or CP-189 for anyone performing UT, RT, MT, PT or other methods, so many inspectors hold both.

Is the BLS salary figure for quality control inspectors useful for API inspectors?

Only as a floor and for comparing regions. The category is dominated by manufacturing inspection roles, so it understates pay for certified mechanical integrity inspectors.

Why do Glassdoor, ZipRecruiter and Indeed show different API inspector pay?

They use different inputs (job postings versus self-reported pay), different definitions (base versus total pay) and different dates. Check the method note and the date on each page before you compare them.
